tasks.title: Mutation-testing scaffold (mutmut, pilot-first)
tasks.verification_command: mutmut run && mutmut results --all true (with pyproject.toml's [tool.mutmut] config)
tasks.oracle_tier_actually_executed: real pilot run in a python:3.12-slim container against src/libipynb/codec/writer.py (the smallest of the 4 hot modules, per this taskcard's own pilot-first mandate): 268 mutants, 186 killed, 61 survived, 21 no-tests, 75.3% score (killed/(killed+survived)). Pilot went through 3 real structural incompatibility classes before reaching a working state, each fixed via mutmut's own intended mechanism rather than forced around: (1) 3 tests asserting libipynb's import origin IS site-packages, structurally incompatible with mutmut's copy-and-mutate execution model -- deselected individually; (2) 2 tests reading repo-root files (.gitlab-ci.yml, scripts/fetch_fixture.py, plans/state.json) mutmut's mutants/ tree doesn't copy by default -- fixed via also_copy for the 2 simple files, the 2 requiring nested directories (plans/state.json, scripts/fetch_fixture.py -- also_copy uses shutil.copy2, which does not create intermediate directories) had their owning test files ignored instead, since both are governance/script metadata orthogonal to writer.py's own behavior; (3) THE load-bearing fix: pytest-cov (installed transitively via the test extra) auto-registers as a pytest plugin and conflicts with mutmut's own internal coverage.py instrumentation, making every single mutant report '<no tests>' (pytest exit code 5) regardless of real coverage -- fixed with `-p no:cov`, confirmed by re-running and getting real kill/survive results immediately after. A second real bug was caught and fixed in the accompanying mutation.yml CI workflow before commit: `mutmut results` with no flag silently omits killed mutants from its output by default (only showing survived/no-tests), which would have made the score-gate script always compute killed=0 and always fail -- fixed with `mutmut results --all true`, verified against the real 268-mutant dataset (186/61/21, exactly matching the pilot run) before committing.

tasks.title: v3->v4 legacy notebook import (decision-gated)
tasks.verification_command: pytest tests/unit/test_doc_drift.py -v --tb=short (no drift check exists for this specific decision beyond README consistency)
tasks.note: DECISION: EXCLUDE native v3 import, per the mission's own explicit 'unless evidence justifies inclusion' default posture. Investigation performed before deciding, not skipped: (1) confirmed directly against the installed nbformat==5.10.4 package that nbformat 4 has been Jupyter's default format since 2015 (over a decade before this writing) -- nbformat.current_nbformat == 4; (2) confirmed nbformat itself still ships and maintains the full v1->v2->v3->v4 upgrade chain (nbformat.v3.upgrade, nbformat.read(as_version=4)) specifically for this legacy case; (3) empirically verified the escape hatch actually works, not just assumed: constructed a real, structurally-plausible nbformat v3 document (worksheets/cells/prompt_number-shaped, the genuine legacy schema, not a guess) and confirmed nbformat.reads(src, as_version=4) correctly auto-upgrades it to nbformat 4.5 with cells translated correctly. Given (a) any actively-maintained v3 notebook would already have been auto-upgraded by Jupyter itself over the last decade, making genuine new v3 input vanishingly rare, and (b) the reference implementation this project already treats as its own schema/oracle authority (nbformat) already solves this exact problem and is a natural, low-friction escape hatch, re-implementing v3 parsing natively here would duplicate an already-solved, low-value problem rather than add real capability. Documented in README.md's 'Supported Versions' section (new paragraph + a working code example) rather than left as a silent gap.

tasks.title: Mutation-after-access audit (result-object immutability sweep)
tasks.oracle_tier_actually_executed: A dedicated investigation agent swept all 62 @dataclass definitions across the codebase for the LIBIPYNB-Q9 bug class (a frozen=True dataclass exposing a live, directly mutable field). 4 real, independently-reproduced findings, all fixed: (1, HIGH) model/parameters.py's InjectedParameter.value aliased the same list/dict object just written into document.raw['metadata']['papermill']['parameters'] -- mutating a report field corrupted the live document, no private-field access needed. (2, HIGH) model/metadata.py's 6 classes (KernelSpecMetadata, LanguageInfoMetadata, AuthorMetadata, JupyterCellMetadata, SlideshowMetadata, ExecutionMetadata) had a bare, directly-mutable _raw dict field re-read fresh by extras()/to_dict() on every call -- an in-place mutation changed what those methods returned afterward, contradicting the module's own 'Read-only typed metadata snapshots' claim; also found and fixed the same gap on LanguageInfoMetadata.codemirror_mode (a public field). (3, MEDIUM-HIGH) model/diff.py's NotebookDiff._target_snapshot had no accessor property at all (unlike NotebookPatch) and was directly mutable -- mutating it before to_patch() propagated through to apply()'s actual output on a real document. (4, MEDIUM) execution/options.py's ExecutionOptions.extra_env was not copied at all, aliasing the caller's dict; adapters/jupyter_execute.py reads it fresh on every execute() call, so mutating between two execute() calls sharing one options instance would silently change the second run's kernel environment. A single-level types.MappingProxyType wrap was tried first for findings 2-4 and found genuinely insufficient (demonstrated live): it only blocks the TOP level -- proxy['metadata'] still returns an unwrapped, fully mutable nested dict, and a notebook snapshot is exactly this kind of multi-level structure. Built a new shared helper, _internal/immutable.py (deep_freeze/deep_thaw), that recursively converts dict->MappingProxyType and list->tuple at every level, with deep_thaw as the inverse (copy.deepcopy cannot be used directly on a MappingProxyType). 2 findings deliberately left unfixed with recorded reasoning: Diagnostic.details (dead code path, no in-repo caller ever passes it) and adapters/export.py's ExportResult.metadata (already reviewed and deliberately left mutable under LIBIPYNB-Q11a, no demonstrated leak). 19 new regression tests across 5 files, each confirmed against the actual pre-fix mutation path (live negative-control repro or direct tracing). tasks.title: NbconvertExporter's binary-output path never validates output-file content, only its existence
tasks.objective: src/libipynb/adapters/export.py's NbconvertExporter binary-output path (fmt='pdf'/other binary formats) writes to --output-dir and reads the resulting file back, but only ever checks output_path.is_file() -- never that the content is non-empty or looks like the claimed format (e.g. a PDF's %PDF- magic bytes). A 'success exit code, file exists, but truncated/garbage content' scenario -- a real, realistic failure mode for a broken/incomplete LaTeX distribution emitting a stub or corrupted PDF -- is neither implemented nor tested, and would currently be reported as a successful export with corrupt binary content rather than a clear NotebookError. Distinct from the already-covered 'reported success but no output file at all' case (test_missing_output_file_after_a_reported_success_raises_a_clear_error).
tasks.rollback: revert; new validation logic + regression test, isolated to NbconvertExporter's binary-output path

tasks.title: validate() can still leak an uncaught RecursionError from find_non_finite_floats if max_nesting_depth is explicitly set above 1000
tasks.objective: validation/validator.py's validate() calls enforce_structure() first (bounding depth per the caller's configured max_nesting_depth), then find_non_finite_floats() (which has its own independent, hard-coded _MAX_DEPTH=1000 backstop, documented in _internal/finiteness.py as existing specifically because 'the two current call sites (validate(), probe()) both already run enforce_structure first, which bounds depth before this function ever runs'). That ordering assumption breaks if a caller explicitly configures max_nesting_depth above 1000: enforce_structure no longer trips before find_non_finite_floats's own backstop does, and validate()'s except clauses (ResourceLimitError, UnicodeEncodeError) do not catch RecursionError -- so a document nested deeper than 1000 levels crashes validate() with an uncaught RecursionError instead of returning the intended structured ValidationReport with an IPYNB_RESOURCE_LIMIT (or similar) diagnostic. Reproduced directly: NotebookResourceLimits(max_nesting_depth=5000) against a 2000-level-deep document raises RecursionError out of validate() rather than returning a report. Narrower than LIBIPYNB-Q55 (only reachable with an explicit above-1000 override, not the default 64) and a distinct fix target (validate()'s own exception-handling completeness, not enforce_structure's container-type coverage) -- found while empirically verifying Q55's fix, deliberately not folded into that commit.
tasks.rollback: revert; likely either an added except RecursionError clause in validate() or a probe() equivalent, plus a regression test -- isolated, no other behavior touched
tasks.discovered_by: this session's own empirical verification of LIBIPYNB-Q55's fix (testing an edge case -- an explicit max_nesting_depth override above find_non_finite_floats's own hard-coded backstop -- not part of Q55's own stated scope)
